abstract: Lashkari, Li, Qiu and Thompson (MIT FutureTech, 2026) build a task-based theory of automation in which AI adoption has task-level fixed costs (model training or fine-tuning), so a task's comparative advantage for AI depends on production scale as well as marginal cost. They quantify the model for computer vision. They estimate fine-tuning scaling laws, use LLM-generated measures of task complexity and error tolerance to infer compute costs for every vision-related task, and calibrate to the September 2023 Census BTOS, when 0.5% of firms (2.4% employment-weighted) reported using computer vision. With projected declines in compute prices, adoption follows an S-curve: 4.7% of firms (12.2% employment-weighted) by 2025 and 22.8% (59.5%) by 2035, with larger firms automating first. Scale accounts for roughly 63% of cross-task variation in AI comparative advantage (about 60% even by 2050). Real output rises 0.1% to 1.7% above the 2023 baseline between 2025 and 2035 (about 16 basis points a year) and about 7% by 2075. Real wages rise throughout. The labor share is U-shaped: it falls while labor and vision AI are gross substitutes, then recovers once the aggregate elasticity drops below one. Retail, arts/entertainment and accommodation/food services are the most automated sectors in 2023, but the sector ranking reshuffles over time.
keyFindings: 22.8% of US firms (59.5% employment-weighted) projected to use computer-vision AI by 2035, up from a calibrated 0.6% (2.4%) in 2023
+1.7% real output above the 2023 baseline by 2035 from computer vision alone (about 16 bp of growth per year 2025-2035); about +7% by 2075
Real wages increase throughout the projected transition; the labor share follows a U-shape
About 63% of cross-task variation in AI comparative advantage in 2023 comes from scale (fixed-cost amortization), not marginal cost
Early adoption is a poor guide to where automation ends up: sector rankings reorder substantially over time
methodology: Quantitative task-based general-equilibrium model with task-level fixed (training) and marginal (inference) automation costs. Scaling law estimated from a vision-model fine-tuning experiment; task complexity and error tolerance from LLM-generated measures; occupation-industry weights from 2023 OEWS. Calibrated to Sept 2023 BTOS computer-vision adoption (Bonney et al. 2024); projections 2023-2075 under trend declines in compute prices.
qualifiers: Tier 1 by repo working-paper convention (unrefereed; strict rubric would be T2). Caveats: covers computer vision only, not LLMs or AI broadly; all forward values are model projections that depend on assumed compute-price declines and calibration choices; adoption is an extensive-margin measure (share of firms automating more than 10% of vision-task varieties); the model is static per period and does not model displacement or transition frictions for workers.
